name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning framework, maintained by the Keras team, that provides a high-level API for building and training neural networks. It runs on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO, letting one codebase target multiple backends. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that Keras 3 is a current standard, with over 2.5 million developers and production use at Waymo and YouTube, though backend-specific performance varies by model.

sections.body: Keras is an open-source deep learning framework written in Python, made by the Keras team and hosted at github.com/keras-team/keras under the Apache-2.0 licence. Its official site describes it as deep learning for humans, and the repository shows a last push in October 2026 with roughly 64,350 stars. Keras 3.0, the current major release, sits at the model-building layer of the AI stack. It is not a numerical backend itself. Instead, it provides the high-level API for defining layers, models, losses, metrics, optimizers, and training loops, and it runs those workflows on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference only. That places it between the raw tensor libraries and the application code a developer writes.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras covers the concrete jobs of deep learning work: training, evaluation, inference, data preprocessing, and model saving. The official guides show image classification with MNIST, autoencoders built with the functional API, transfer learning for flower classification, and text generation with a mini-GPT trained through KerasHub. Built-in methods such as fit(), evaluate(), and predict() handle training and inference loops, and they accept NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. Keras is strongest when a team wants one readable codebase that can move between backends, and when built-in layers and standard workflows cover the model. The site notes that JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU, though results vary by model, and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed for human readability, and the official site supports beginners with step-by-step guides on the Sequential model, the functional API, and built-in training methods. The Sequential guide explains that a plain stack of layers is the right starting point, that layers need to know their input shape to create weights, and that specifying the input shape in advance is recommended. The functional API guide then introduces non-linear topology, shared layers, and multiple inputs or outputs. A learner needs basic Python and some familiarity with tensors and neural network concepts such as loss functions, optimizers, and metrics. The site does not present Keras as a replacement for understanding the underlying mathematics, and it does not claim that prior systems knowledge is unnecessary.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around Keras is broad. Keras 3 implements the full Keras API across TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch, including over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides cross-backend operations such as ops.matmul, ops.sum, ops.stack, ops.einsum, and neural network functions such as ops.softmax, ops.binary_crossentropy, and ops.conv. KerasHub supplies pretrained models and layers, including the TokenAndPositionEmbedding and TransformerDecoder layers used in the mini-GPT example. The keras.distribution namespace handles model and data parallelism, currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon. The official site offers guides, examples, and API documentation, and the repository has a large star count, though the facts given do not include contributor counts or forum activity.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production work, and the trade-off is mostly about which backend you choose. The Sequential and functional APIs make prototyping fast, with fit(), evaluate(), and predict() handling standard training and inference without custom loops. For production, Keras 3 adds backend choice and the distribution API for model parallelism, data parallelism, and combinations of both. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function. The cost is that performance depends on the backend and the model: the site says JAX typically leads on GPU, TPU, and CPU, but results vary, and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU. The distribution API is also not yet available on every backend, which limits some large-scale training patterns today.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The official Keras 3 page states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. That makes it a current standard rather than a legacy choice, and it is the high-level API for TensorFlow, JAX, and PyTorch workflows. For someone choosing what to learn for work, Keras offers a transferable skill: a model written with built-in layers can run on all supported backends, and existing tf.keras models that use built-in layers can start running in JAX and PyTorch right away. The facts and the site do not provide salary data, job posting counts, or a breakdown of adoption by industry, so claims about hiring demand beyond these named users would not be supported.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is a Python framework, and it is typically used alongside JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch rather than instead of them. The polyglot pattern is that Keras supplies the model definition and training loop, while the chosen backend supplies the numerical execution and hardware acceleration. Keras can also act as a low-level cross-framework language for custom components such as layers, models, or metrics that can then be used in native JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch workflows from one codebase. The keras.ops namespace is the bridge that makes this work: as long as custom code uses only ops from keras.ops, custom layers will run on JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow with the same code. OpenVINO is supported for inference only, so it fits the deployment side rather than training.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Keras is not the right tool for every model. The Sequential guide states that a Sequential model is not appropriate for non-linear topology such as residual connections or multi-branch models, and those cases require the functional API or subclassing. The distribution API is currently implemented for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch described as coming soon, so teams that need model or data parallelism on those backends face a gap. Backend performance is not uniform, and the site itself says results vary from model to model. The official material does not say how many contributors maintain the project, how frequently releases occur, or how the framework compares with alternatives on benchmarks beyond the backend notes. It also does not settle questions about long-term support timelines or commercial support options.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
